About This Part
Volume 7D develops the application platform layer of Azure. Parts A through C established identity, governance,
infrastructure, networking, storage, databases, analytics, and migration. This part turns those foundations into
secure delivery platforms for containers, Kubernetes, web applications, functions, APIs, messaging, event
distribution, and orchestrated workflows. The engineering objective is not to deploy a demo that responds once. It is to create repeatable application
platforms with immutable artifacts, controlled identity, private connectivity, observable releases, back-
pressure, idempotency, dead-letter handling, rollback, tested recovery, and explicit ownership. Every service is
evaluated as part of a system rather than as an isolated product. Safety, Security, and Cost Controls

Chapter 31 - Azure Container Registry and Container Supply-Chain
Engineering
Building a trusted artifact system for images, OCI artifacts, regional distribution, promotion, and controlled
runtime consumption
Learning Objectives



31.1 A Registry Is a Production Control Point
Azure Container Registry (ACR) stores private container images and other OCI artifacts, but its operational role
is broader than storage. It is the boundary between build systems and runtime platforms. A weak registry
design allows mutable tags, unknown base images, broad push permissions, and uncontrolled public
dependencies to enter production.

Create separate repositories or registries according to trust boundaries, ownership, compliance, and blast
radius - not merely according to team preference.

Use one-way promotion. Build once, identify the artifact by digest, and promote the same digest through
development, test, staging, and production.

Do not allow production clusters to pull directly from arbitrary public registries. Import or cache approved
public artifacts through ACR and retain evidence of origin.

Use retention and purge policies carefully.

31.3 Immutable Promotion and Supply-Chain Evidence
1. Build in an isolated, reproducible pipeline using a reviewed Dockerfile and pinned base-image digest.
2. Run source, dependency, secret, infrastructure, and image scans; record exceptions with owners and expiry
dates.
3. Generate an SBOM and provenance record. Store evidence with the immutable release artifact.
4. Push once, capture the image digest, and use the digest in deployment manifests or a signed release bundle.
5. Promote by registry-side import or metadata approval rather than rebuilding for each environment.
6. Deploy with a runtime identity that has pull-only access and verify the admitted digest.
az acr create -g rg-platform -n acrcontoso001 --sku Premium
az acr import -n acrcontoso001 \
--source docker.io/library/nginx:1.27 \
--image approved/nginx:1.27
az acr repository show-tags -n acrcontoso001 \
--repository approved/nginx --detail
Tags remain useful human labels, but they are not immutable identities. Release records should name the
digest, source commit, pipeline run, policy result, deployment environment, and rollback digest.

2. When is ACR Premium justified?

Chapter 32 - Azure Kubernetes Service Production Engineering
Operating managed Kubernetes with secure identity, networking, scaling, upgrades, policy, observability, and
platform ownership
Learning Objectives

32.1 Managed Kubernetes Still Requires a Platform Team
AKS manages the Kubernetes control plane and integrates Azure services, but the customer still owns workload
architecture, node pools, Kubernetes objects, network policy, identity, resource requests, upgrades, admission
controls, data protection, and incident response. A production AKS service therefore needs a defined platform
product, not an unmanaged shared cluster. Boundary

32.2 Cluster, Node-Pool, and Network Design
Use system node pools for critical add-ons and separate user node pools by workload characteristics, trust,
architecture, operating system, GPU need, or disruption tolerance. Availability zones, multiple replicas, topology
spread constraints, anti-affinity, and PodDisruptionBudgets reduce correlated failure, but only when resource
capacity exists to reschedule workloads.

Choose Azure CNI mode and network architecture from IP capacity, network-policy, observability, and
connectivity requirements. Reserve address space for growth and upgrades.

Use private clusters or API server VNet integration where operational access paths, DNS, and incident
response are designed in advance.

Expose applications through a controlled ingress or Gateway API implementation. Terminate TLS with
managed certificate processes and restrict internal services.

Use network policies and Azure perimeter controls together. Kubernetes policy does not replace NSGs,
firewall, private endpoints, or application authorization.
32.3 Identity and Workload Access
Microsoft Entra Workload ID maps a Kubernetes service account to an Azure identity using projected service-
account tokens and federated credentials. It replaces deprecated pod-identity approaches and avoids

assignment at the narrowest practical scope.

az aks show -g rg-aks -n aks-prod \

Cluster administrator access, Kubernetes authorization, Azure resource access, and container-registry pull
access are separate decisions. Troubleshooting must identify which identity and which authorization layer
denied the request.

can recommend or adjust requests; cluster autoscaler changes node capacity. These mechanisms interact. Incorrect requests, missing metrics, restrictive disruption budgets, unavailable IP addresses, or node-pool limits
can prevent safe scaling.

Use supported Kubernetes versions, automatic or controlled upgrade channels, maintenance windows,
preproduction rings, surge capacity, and workload compatibility tests.

Configure requests, limits, startup/readiness/liveness probes, PodDisruptionBudgets, topology spread,
graceful termination, and deployment rollback.

Collect control-plane logs, Container Insights or managed Prometheus metrics, application traces, audit
data, and Kubernetes events with retention appropriate to incident needs.


33.2 Environments, Revisions, Ingress, and Traffic
A Container Apps environment is the security, networking, and observability boundary for multiple apps and
jobs. Revisions are immutable snapshots of revision-scope configuration. Single-revision mode simplifies
replacement; multiple-revision mode supports traffic splitting, canary releases, and side-by-side validation.

Use internal environments or restricted ingress when services should not be public.

Keep secrets and environment-specific settings outside images. Prefer managed identity and Key Vault
integration patterns.

Use revision labels and explicit traffic weights for progressive delivery; observe errors, latency, and
business outcomes before promotion.

Design egress, private DNS, VNet integration, private endpoints, and downstream firewall rules as one path.
33.3 KEDA Scaling, Jobs, and Dapr
Container Apps uses KEDA-supported scale triggers. HTTP concurrency, queue depth, event-stream lag, CPU,
memory, and custom scalers can drive replica count. Scale-to-zero saves cost but introduces cold-start and
connection behavior that must fit the SLO. Minimum replicas or workload profiles may be needed for latency-
sensitive services.

Dapr can provide service invocation, state, pub/sub, bindings, and secrets abstractions, but it adds runtime
behavior and configuration ownership. Use it where the portability and consistency benefit exceeds the added
operational surface. Container Apps Jobs are preferable for finite tasks; implement checkpointing and
idempotency because retries can repeat work.

Observe revision health, replica count, scaler decisions, ingress latency, console/system logs, job executions,
Dapr sidecars, and downstream dependencies. Define maximum replicas to protect budgets and dependencies,
but ensure limits do not silently cap required throughput. For dedicated workload profiles, track reserved
capacity utilization.

Test cold starts, scale-from-zero, maximum-scale behavior, and dependency saturation.

Retain failed job logs and payload identifiers for replay while protecting sensitive content.

Use image digests and ACR managed identity. Avoid registry username/password secrets.

Delete inactive revisions and abandoned environments only after rollback and forensic retention

Operating managed web applications and APIs with deployment slots, identity, private connectivity, scaling,
configuration, and recovery
Learning Objectives

Design App Service plans, apps, slots, scaling, availability zones, and regional topology.

Separate inbound private access from outbound VNet integration and dependency connectivity.


34.1 App Service as a Managed Application Platform
Azure App Service runs web applications and APIs without exposing VM administration. The App Service plan
defines regional compute, operating system, scaling boundary, and cost. Multiple apps can share a plan, which
improves utilization but also creates noisy-neighbor, scaling, and blast-radius considerations.

Separate production from non-production plans and isolate workloads with different scaling, compliance,
or failure characteristics.

Use deployment slots on supported tiers to stage releases, warm dependencies, validate health, and swap
configuration safely.

Use zone-redundant plans where supported and justified, but design regional recovery independently.

Keep local file-system assumptions minimal. Store durable state in managed data services.

resources in or through a virtual network. They solve different directions and are often both required.
